<title>Korvath Greenhouses: interview on the irrigation project</title>
<transcript>
[0] Odalys Brenner: Thanks for making the time, both of you.
[1] Odalys Brenner: Can you hear me all right?
[2] Teodor Vance: Loud and clear.
[3] Priya Lindqvist: Yes, fine here.
[4] Priya Lindqvist: Sorry about the fans in the background, I'm in the packing hall.
[5] Odalys Brenner: No problem at all.
[6] Odalys Brenner: For readers who don't know Korvath Greenhouses, give me the short version.
[7] Teodor Vance: We grow tomatoes and cucumbers under glass.
[8] Teodor Vance: We have two sites, Ellsmoor and Farrow Bank.
[9] Teodor Vance: Ellsmoor is the bigger one, 14 hectares.
[10] Odalys Brenner: And you are the operations director.
[11] Teodor Vance: I am.
[12] Teodor Vance: Priya is our head grower at Ellsmoor.
[13] Odalys Brenner: The reason I called is the irrigation project.
[14] Odalys Brenner: When did it start?
[15] Teodor Vance: We started in March 2025 with a pilot in one block.
[16] Teodor Vance: That block is 2 hectares.
[17] Odalys Brenner: What were you doing before the pilot?
[18] Priya Lindqvist: Fixed timers.
[19] Priya Lindqvist: Every block got 9 irrigation cycles a day, at set times, whatever the weather was doing.
[20] Odalys Brenner: Whatever the weather.
[21] Priya Lindqvist: More or less.
[22] Priya Lindqvist: We would adjust by hand on very hot days, but the schedule was the schedule.
[23] Odalys Brenner: And what replaced it?
[24] Priya Lindqvist: Moisture sensors in the growing substrate.
[25] Priya Lindqvist: The system waters a row when that row is actually drying out, not when the clock says so.
[26] Odalys Brenner: How many sensors are we talking about?
[27] Teodor Vance: Across Ellsmoor, 420.
[28] Teodor Vance: The pilot block had 60 of them.
[29] Odalys Brenner: What did the pilot show you?
[30] Priya Lindqvist: That we had been watering at the wrong times.
[31] Priya Lindqvist: The plants were telling us they were thirsty at eleven, and we were watering them at nine.
[32] Odalys Brenner: That's a good line.
[33] Odalys Brenner: Can I quote that?
[34] Priya Lindqvist: Go ahead.
[35] Odalys Brenner: Let's talk numbers.
[36] Odalys Brenner: What happened to water use?
[37] Teodor Vance: On tomatoes we went from 22 litres of water per kilo of fruit to 15 litres.
[38] Odalys Brenner: So about a third less.
[39] Teodor Vance: About a third, yes.
[40] Teodor Vance: That is the Ellsmoor figure for the season after the full rollout.
[41] Odalys Brenner: When was the full rollout finished?
[42] Teodor Vance: October 2025.
[43] Teodor Vance: Every block at Ellsmoor has been on sensors since then.
[44] Odalys Brenner: Did anything else move?
[45] Odalys Brenner: Fertiliser, for example.
[46] Teodor Vance: Fertiliser spend is down 11 percent.
[47] Teodor Vance: Less water through the substrate means less feed washed out with it.
[48] Odalys Brenner: And yield?
[49] Teodor Vance: Flat.
[50] Teodor Vance: I would not claim a yield gain from this.
[51] Priya Lindqvist: I'd put it a bit differently.
[52] Priya Lindqvist: Cucumber yield was up 4 percent in the sensor blocks.
[53] Teodor Vance: It was, but that is one season, and we changed the cucumber variety in the same year.
[54] Priya Lindqvist: That's fair.
[55] Priya Lindqvist: I think the sensors helped, but I can't prove it from one season.
[56] Odalys Brenner: So you two don't fully agree on that one.
[57] Teodor Vance: We agree on the water.
[58] Teodor Vance: We disagree a little on the cucumbers.
[59] Odalys Brenner: What did the whole thing cost?
[60] Teodor Vance: 310,000 euros for Ellsmoor, including the sensors, the controllers and the installation.
[61] Odalys Brenner: And the payback?
[62] Teodor Vance: We expect about three years.
[63] Teodor Vance: Most of that comes from water and fertiliser, not from yield.
[64] Odalys Brenner: Did anything go wrong?
[65] Priya Lindqvist: Yes.
[66] Priya Lindqvist: In June a firmware update knocked out 60 sensors for two days.
[67] Odalys Brenner: What did you do for those two days?
[68] Priya Lindqvist: We put those rows back on the old timers.
[69] Priya Lindqvist: That's the fallback, and it worked, but it was a nervous couple of days.
[70] Teodor Vance: We now test every update on one row before it goes anywhere else.
[71] Odalys Brenner: What about the people side?
[72] Odalys Brenner: Did anyone lose their job to a sensor?
[73] Teodor Vance: No.
[74] Teodor Vance: Nobody was laid off.
[75] Priya Lindqvist: Three of our growers were retrained to read the sensor data.
[76] Priya Lindqvist: Their job changed from walking the rows with a hand meter to checking the rows the system flags.
[77] Odalys Brenner: Do they like it?
[78] Priya Lindqvist: Two of them do.
[79] Priya Lindqvist: One still walks the rows anyway, and honestly I don't mind that.
[80] Odalys Brenner: What's next?
[81] Teodor Vance: Farrow Bank.
[82] Teodor Vance: We plan to install the same system there in spring 2026.
[83] Odalys Brenner: Is that decided or is that a hope?
[84] Teodor Vance: The budget is approved.
[85] Teodor Vance: The installation dates are not fixed yet.
[86] Odalys Brenner: Anything beyond the sensors?
[87] Teodor Vance: We are also building a rainwater tank at Ellsmoor.
[88] Teodor Vance: It will hold 5,000 cubic metres.
[89] Priya Lindqvist: The idea is that less of what we use comes from the mains in the first place.
[90] Odalys Brenner: Last question.
[91] Odalys Brenner: If another grower asked whether to do this, what would you tell them?
[92] Priya Lindqvist: Start with one block.
[93] Priya Lindqvist: We learned more from the pilot than from any brochure.
[94] Teodor Vance: And keep the timers.
[95] Teodor Vance: You will need them the day the sensors go down.
[96] Odalys Brenner: That's a good place to stop.
[97] Odalys Brenner: Thank you both.
[98] Teodor Vance: Thank you.
[99] Priya Lindqvist: Thanks, Odalys.
</transcript>

points.text: Korvath Greenhouses grows tomatoes and cucumbers under glass at two sites, Ellsmoor (14 hectares, the bigger one) and Farrow Bank.
The irrigation project began in March 2025 with a pilot in one 2-hectare block, which had 60 sensors.
Before the project, every block got 9 fixed-timer irrigation cycles a day regardless of weather, with occasional manual adjustment on very hot days.
Moisture sensors in the growing substrate now trigger watering of a row when it is actually drying out; Ellsmoor has 420 sensors.
The pilot showed they had been watering at the wrong times: plants signalled thirst at eleven while they were watered at nine.
Tomato water use at Ellsmoor fell from 22 to 15 litres per kilo of fruit (about a third), for the season after full rollout.
Full rollout at Ellsmoor finished in October 2025, and every block has been on sensors since.
Fertiliser spend is down 11 percent, because less water through the substrate washes out less feed.
Overall yield was flat according to Vance, who would not claim a yield gain.
Lindqvist cited a 4 percent cucumber yield rise in sensor blocks; Vance noted it was one season with a cucumber variety change, and Lindqvist conceded she can't prove the sensors caused it.
The Ellsmoor project cost 310,000 euros including sensors, controllers and installation; payback is expected in about three years, mostly from water and fertiliser savings rather than yield.
In June a firmware update knocked out 60 sensors for two days; those rows went back on the old timers as a fallback, and updates are now tested on one row first.
Nobody was laid off; three growers were retrained to read sensor data and check flagged rows instead of walking rows with a hand meter. Two like it, one still walks the rows.
Farrow Bank is planned to get the same system in spring 2026; the budget is approved but installation dates are not fixed.
Korvath is building a 5,000 cubic metre rainwater tank at Ellsmoor to reduce mains water use.
Advice to other growers: start with one block, and keep the timers as a fallback.
